Figure 1:Overview of this work.(1) The new paradigm: a coding agent turns a recording of a real event into a program that simulates it.
Every simulation frame here is rendered by re-running a program that the Codex agent wrote for the input video recording.(2) Real2SimLab runs the program that a method writes, scores its output with the scorer of the benchmark, and creates training data and reward annotations.
(3) Awesome-Real2Sim organizes nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers according to what they deliver or ask for.

Figure 2:Why a shared platform helps.(a) Without a shared platform, benchmarks differ in what they provide to a method, what they ask the method to deliver, and how they score the output. Every pair of a method and a benchmark thus requires its own adapter to run.
(b) Real2SimLab makes the delivered program into the interface between methods and benchmarks. So each method and each benchmark is integrated only once.

Figure 3:A roadmap of real-to-simulation, from Awesome-Real2Sim.Selected methods (gray) and benchmarks (violet) are placed by the month of their first arXiv version (for Galileo, which has none, by the month of its conference).
Each card names the institution and what the paper delivers or asks for.
The methods deliver many kinds of results, such as physical twins (fitted or assigned), simulation-ready assets, scene twins, learned simulators, and simulation programs.
One recent trend is that coding agents write simulation programs, and recent benchmarks such as 4DCodeBench, PhysCodeGym, and Video2World are proposed to evaluate these agents.

Figure 4:Architecture of Real2SimLab.A method-wise adapter (left) passes the visible part of a task to a method and collects its deliverable, and a benchmark-wise adapter (right) turns the data of a benchmark into tasks.
In between (center), Real2SimLab fixes one task format.
It builds each deliverable in a sandbox, freezes it, re-runs it offline, and scores it with the protocol of the benchmark.
All results are stored in one record format and reported in one scorecard. Training tasks use the same format as evaluation tasks, and their rewards are computed by the scoring code of evaluation (Section5).

Figure 5:The benchmarks that Real2SimLab adapts so far.Each card shows what a method sees, what it delivers, and how the deliverable is scored.
Of the 6 existing benchmarks, 5 keep their official scorers, while IRIS (markedLab) and our synthetic suite (markedexact truth) use the reproduction skill of Real2SimLab.
New benchmarks and recordings of users are added by converting them into tasks of the shared format (Section3.1).

Figure 6:The training data pipeline.(1) Training tasks come from recordings of users, from a released training split when a benchmark has one, or from our generator of synthetic scenes, and they use the format of evaluation tasks.
(2) The overlap check removes every task that shows the recording of an evaluation task, by comparing thumbnails of the frames in which something moves, at every time offset.
In the example, a PhysCodeGym clip, treated here as a candidate for training, contains the hidden test video of a Physics-IQ evaluation task, starting 3 s into the clip.
(3) The dataset holds the tasks and the runs on them, and each run holds a program, its reward, and the log of the agent.
(4) A trainer of the user’s choice trains a method offline on the dataset, or online with rewards from the evaluation code.
(5) Real2SimLab evaluates the trained method as in Section3, but skips the evaluation tasks that overlap its training tasks.
Real2SimLab provides all steps but the trainer; we have not yet trained a model with them.
